stories.headline: COP31 final day wrangles over fossil-fuel cuts and climate finance
stories.summary: The COP31 summit in Antalya, Türkiye, entered its final day with negotiators still divided over the depth of fossil-fuel cuts, the scale of climate finance and the fairness of the second Global Stocktake (GST2). The latest draft cover decision retains an electrification goal — raising electricity's share of total final energy use to 35% by 2035, the '35x35' target — but in weakened form, reflecting resistance over money and equity. Developing countries argue that ambition cannot be raised without predictable finance and technology transfer, while commentary focused on smallholders stresses that pledges must translate into accessible credit and adaptation support. The outcome will shape how the Paris Agreement's ratchet mechanism and the principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) are applied in the next round of NDCs.
stories.whyItMatters: COP cover decisions and the Global Stocktake set the benchmark against which India's NDCs, its net-zero-by-2070 pathway and its climate-finance demands are judged. It links GS-III environment content with GS-II global-governance questions on equity and multilateral reform.

perspectives.take: Frames the global electrification push (35% of final energy use by 2035) as colliding with disputes over money and fairness, noting the latest draft may dilute the goal.

stories.headline: Trump courts Xi and Putin as middle powers, India chart multipolar course
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump's outreach to Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, and the prospect of a trilateral summit among the three leaders, has revived debate over whether great-power bargaining can deliver progress on nuclear weapons and global order. Reuters reports that middle powers are not waiting on the big three, instead pursuing their own diplomatic and strategic arrangements. In Asia, the Quad — India, the US, Japan and Australia — is assessed by ORF as having gained renewed purpose through its Manila engagement. Indian commentary is split on the opportunity: one strand urges New Delhi to construct an Asian identity in which China participates without dominating, positioning India as a bridge between the Global South, the West and Central Asia; another argues that groupings such as the G20 and BRICS cannot substitute for legitimate multilateral forums and that India should aim to become a 'fourth pole'. Deccan Herald frames the moment more sceptically, as a spectacle of great-power politics whose consequences for middle and smaller states remain unsettled.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the core of India's strategic autonomy and multi-alignment: how New Delhi balances the Quad, BRICS and SCO, and its Global South leadership, when the US, China and Russia negotiate directly among themselves.

stories.headline: Saudi coalition strikes Hodeidah; Houthis fire at Riyadh as Iran signals diplomacy
stories.summary: Saudi Arabia said it intercepted three Houthi missiles aimed at Riyadh, shortly after the Saudi-led coalition announced strikes on Yemen's Hodeidah port, which it described as a hub for smuggling weapons and ballistic missiles. The Houthis responded by threatening Jeddah and other Red Sea ports, widening the risk to maritime traffic through the region. On the diplomatic track, Iran's Foreign Minister Araqchi said Tehran wants diplomacy to end the war, but Trump dismissed the terms as unacceptable, leaving negotiations stalled. Indian analytical commentary reads the crisis through China's regional positioning, while regional and Western outlets foreground the escalation's security and shipping fallout.
stories.whyItMatters: The flare-up ties together core GS-II themes — West Asia instability, maritime chokepoints and great-power bargaining — and bears directly on India's energy imports, westward trade routes and Gulf diaspora. It is a live test of India's multi-alignment in a region where it must engage Saudi Arabia, Iran and the US simultaneously.

static.topic: Cauvery Basin and Monsoon Dependence

static.whatIsIt: The Cauvery is a peninsular river, rain-fed and dependent on the southwest monsoon. Its basin covers Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry, making water availability seasonal and variable.
static.background: The Indian monsoon delivers about 75% of annual rainfall during June–September. El Niño usually weakens the monsoon; La Niña strengthens it; the Indian Ocean Dipole modulates it. Peninsular rivers are seasonal, unlike Himalayan snow-fed rivers.
static.geography: The Cauvery rises in Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri range (Karnataka), flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and drains into the Bay of Bengal. The Western Ghats influence its catchment.
static.socioEconomic: Agriculture in both states relies heavily on Cauvery water; shortfalls trigger disputes over drinking water, irrigation, and power.
static.whyInNews: Karnataka's Chief Minister cited drinking water scarcity after the Supreme Court dismissed Tamil Nadu's plea for additional Cauvery water.
static.wayForward: Promote rainwater harvesting, micro-irrigation, crop diversification, and basin-level reservoir management to reduce monsoon dependence.
prelimsPointers: Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow-fed); peninsular rivers are seasonal.

TheWire's report uses the anniversary to press questions about the role of India's Supreme Court in the Rohingya deportation litigation, while a second TheWire piece notes that New Delhi has 'taken note' of the ICJ verdict without using the word genocide. Separately, the US Treasury said on November 19 that it had frozen the assets of General Saw Shwe Wah, commander-in-chief of the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), and one of his senior officers, barring Americans from dealing with them. Washington tied the designations to the criminal scam networks operating out of Myanmar's borderlands. Taken together, the developments show judicial and financial pressure converging on Myanmar's military-linked actors.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the reach of international judicial and sanctions mechanisms against atrocity crimes, and the calibration of India's Myanmar policy — a recurring GS-II theme on international institutions and neighbourhood diplomacy.

perspectives.take: Frames the ICJ ruling's anniversary as a domestic accountability question, asking whether the Supreme Court's handling of Rohingya deportation pleas amounts to complicity.
Reads India's carefully worded 'taken note' response as deliberate avoidance of the term genocide, consistent with its long-standing non-interventionist stance.
Reports the US Treasury action factually, foregrounding the sanctions-designation detail and the scam-centre economy rather than the wider human-rights debate.

static.topic: International Court of Justice and the Genocide Convention
static.syllabusNode: Important International Institutions, agencies and fora — their structure and mandate
static.whatIsIt: The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, seated at the Peace Palace in The Hague, with 15 judges elected for nine-year terms. It settles disputes between states and gives advisory opinions to authorised UN bodies.
static.background: Established in 1945 under the UN Charter and the Statute of the ICJ, it succeeded the Permanent Court of International Justice. The 1948 Genocide Convention obliges states to prevent and punish genocide, and Article IX permits disputes to be referred to the ICJ. The Gambia filed a case against Myanmar in November 2019; the Court ordered provisional measures in January 2020 and rejected Myanmar's preliminary objections in July 2022, allowing the case to proceed on the merits.
static.geography: Seat: The Hague, Netherlands; the underlying dispute concerns Myanmar's Rakhine State.
static.socioEconomic: Rohingya displacement into Bangladesh and the wider region, and questions of citizenship and refugee protection in Myanmar.
static.whyInNews: The sixth anniversary of the ICJ's provisional measures order has revived scrutiny of the case and of domestic judicial responses to it.
static.wayForward: Wider acceptance of the Court's compulsory jurisdiction and stronger Security Council follow-through on Article 94 obligations would improve compliance.
prelimsPointers: Only states may be parties to contentious cases before the ICJ; individuals and organisations cannot sue there.
The ICJ has 15 judges, elected by the UN General Assembly and Security Council for nine-year terms and eligible for re-election.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether international judicial bodies can deliver accountability for mass atrocities when enforcement depends on a politically divided Security Council.

static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: structure, independence, judicial review and access to justice
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 and 226 provide writ jurisdiction.
static.socioEconomic: Pendency and vacancies shape access to justice, and PILs have made the Court a forum for refugee and rights claims.
static.whyInNews: TheWire's report on the ICJ ruling's anniversary raises questions about the Supreme Court's record in the Rohingya deportation litigation.
static.wayForward: Address judicial vacancies and backlog while preserving the balance between judicial independence and accountability.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction: disputes between the Centre and states (Article 131).
Advisory jurisdiction is exercised under Article 143.
static.mainsAngle: Examine judicial backlog, vacancies and pendency, and the balance between judicial independence and accountability.

static.topic: India–Myanmar relations and the Rohingya refugee question
static.syllabusNode: India and its neighbourhood — bilateral relations; effect of policies of developed and developing countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: India shares a land border with Myanmar and has historically allowed visa-free movement across it under the Free Movement Regime; the Rohingya, a largely stateless Muslim minority from Rakhine State, have sought refuge in India.
static.background: The Free Movement Regime permitted people living within 16 km of the border to cross without a visa; in 2024 India announced plans to end the FMR and fence the border. India has not joined The Gambia's ICJ case and has consistently avoided the term 'genocide' in its official statements.
static.geography: The India–Myanmar border runs through Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram; Rakhine State lies on Myanmar's western coast.
static.socioEconomic: Refugee inflows, deportation petitions, and the dependence of border communities on cross-border trade and movement.
static.whyInNews: India 'took note' of the ICJ verdict without mentioning genocide, while the US sanctioned a Myanmar armed group leader over scam operations.
static.wayForward: A humane, rules-based refugee framework alongside continued engagement with all stakeholders in Myanmar would balance security and humanitarian concerns.
prelimsPointers: The India–Myanmar border is roughly 1,643 km long and touches four Indian states.
Myanmar is the only ASEAN member with which India shares a land border.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the security and humanitarian dilemmas in India's Myanmar policy, with reference to the Rohingya and the Free Movement Regime.

prelims: The ICJ's provisional measures in The Gambia v. Myanmar were ordered in January 2020, six years before these reports; the Court rejected Myanmar's preliminary objections in July 2022.

The US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) administers such designations; the November 19 action froze the assets of General Saw Shwe Wah, chief of the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), and a senior officer.
India's official response 'took note' of the ICJ verdict but did not use the word 'genocide'.
stories.mainsQuestion: The ICJ's provisional measures in The Gambia v. Myanmar have not ended the persecution of the Rohingya. Examine the limits of international judicial mechanisms in delivering accountability for mass atrocities, and outline India's stated position on the Rohingya question.

stories.headline: AI capital boom: Anthropic listing buzz, Oracle funding, market slide, local pushback
stories.summary: The global AI build-out is now being reported as much through capital markets as through technology. Oracle said its OpenAI infrastructure commitment is fully funded after a final capital raise, indicating that large-scale AI compute spending is still being financed at size. On the same day, a tech stock sell-off — with Anthropic shares sliding and the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory, as reported — showed how heavily broad US indices now ride on AI valuations. Friction is also appearing off the balance sheet: a reported 595 objections to an Anthropic-backed Australian 'AI factory' data centre, and a Business Standard account of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang's abrasive management style, point to land, energy and governance questions inside the supply chain. The Hindu's editorial uses the Anthropic listing moment to argue that India cannot afford silence in a multi-trillion-dollar AI arms race.
stories.whyItMatters: AI capex is now a macro-financial variable, not just a technology theme — valuation concentration, infrastructure financing and local consent are all exam-relevant entry points. For India, the story sharpens questions on AI strategy, capital-market depth and data-centre siting.

perspectives.take: Wire-service neutrality: sticks to the corporate disclosure that Oracle's OpenAI infrastructure deal is fully funded after a final capital raise, with minimal interpretation.
Anglo-American market lens: narrates the day as a sell-off, noting Anthropic's share slide and US indices entering correction territory.
Corporate-governance angle: alleges that Nvidia's Jensen Huang made threats, insults and settlements routine — a leadership-culture and risk story inside the AI supply chain.
Ground-level/community lens: foregrounds 595 objections to an Anthropic-backed Australian data centre, framing AI expansion as a land, energy and local-consent issue.

static.topic: Artificial Intelligence: governance, strategy and India's position
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Developments and their applications; Awareness in the fields of IT
static.whatIsIt: AI refers to systems that perform tasks associated with human cognition — learning, inference, perception and generation. Governance covers compute, data, model safety, competition and accountability.
static.background: The term was coined at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop; expert systems rose in the 1980s, deep learning took off after 2012, and generative AI from 2022 onward. NITI Aayog's National Strategy for AI (2018) was India's first broad policy framework; the IndiaAI Mission was approved in 2024 with an outlay of roughly Rs 10,370 crore, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides the data-governance backbone.
static.geography: Global; India as a compute and talent base
static.socioEconomic: AI adoption affects labour markets, MSME productivity, language inclusion and the digital divide; compute access determines who can build models.
static.whyInNews: Anthropic's move towards a public listing, Oracle's funding of OpenAI infrastructure and a US tech sell-off have turned AI into a capital-markets and strategic-policy story.
static.wayForward: A clear national position on compute procurement, model safety and standards-setting; antitrust and disclosure norms for AI-linked valuations; skilling pipelines and public compute access.
prelimsPointers: NITI Aayog's National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence was released in 2018.
The IndiaAI Mission (2024) is the umbrella national programme for AI compute, datasets and skilling.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was enacted in 2023.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether India's AI policy architecture — mission-mode funding plus data-protection law — is adequate to secure strategic autonomy in a market dominated by a few private firms.

static.topic: Capital markets, IPOs and valuation concentration risk
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Capital Markets; mobilisation of resources
static.whatIsIt: An IPO is a first public offering of shares by a company, moving it from private to listed status and subjecting it to disclosure and listing obligations. Index concentration measures how much a few stocks drive a benchmark.
static.background: SEBI was set up in 1988 and given statutory powers by the SEBI Act, 1992; IPO disclosures are governed by the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018. Global indices such as the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average are market-capitalisation or price weighted, so a handful of large technology firms can dominate movements.
static.socioEconomic: Household savings, pension and mutual fund exposures transmit equity-market corrections to ordinary savers; retail participation has risen sharply via SIPs and demat accounts.
static.whyInNews: Tech stocks sold off, Anthropic shares slid, and the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average were reported to have entered correction territory, illustrating AI-driven index concentration.
static.wayForward: Stronger disclosure on AI-linked revenue and capex commitments; concentration and liquidity monitoring by regulators; investor education on index concentration.
prelimsPointers: A market 'correction' conventionally means a fall of 10% or more from a recent peak; a bear market is a 20% fall.
SEBI is the statutory regulator of India's securities market under the SEBI Act, 1992.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the financial-stability implications of extreme index concentration in technology stocks and the regulatory tools available to securities-market regulators.

static.topic: Data centres: energy demand, water use and local consent
static.whatIsIt: Data centres are facilities housing servers and cooling systems that power cloud and AI workloads; large AI-dedicated campuses are increasingly called 'AI factories'.
static.background: India's data-centre capacity has clustered around Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad, aided by submarine cable landing stations and state incentives. Globally, the growth of hyperscale campuses has made electricity grid connection and water availability the binding constraints.
static.geography: Australia (site of the reported opposition); India's clusters in Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad and Noida
static.socioEconomic: Data centres create construction and technical jobs but raise local concerns over land acquisition, groundwater use, noise and strain on transmission infrastructure.
static.whyInNews: Around 595 objections were reported against an Anthropic-backed 'AI factory' data centre in Australia, signalling local resistance to AI infrastructure.
static.wayForward: Siting norms with mandatory environmental impact assessment, renewable power procurement, water-recycling requirements and benefit-sharing with host communities.
prelimsPointers: Data centres are highly electricity-intensive, and cooling accounts for a significant share of their power and water use.
India's data-centre growth is concentrated near submarine cable landing points such as Mumbai and Chennai.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the AI compute build-out is reshaping energy demand and local environmental politics, and suggest safeguards for siting large data centres in India.

prelims: Oracle stated that its OpenAI infrastructure deal is fully funded after a final capital raise — a statement about financing, not about project completion.
A 'correction' is a fall of 10% or more from a recent peak; the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average were reported to have entered correction territory during the tech sell-off.
About 595 objections were reported against an Anthropic-backed 'AI factory' data centre in Australia, illustrating local-consent friction in AI infrastructure.
Anthropic is an AI model developer; Nvidia is the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — both sit at different points of the same compute value chain.
stories.mainsQuestion: The race to build AI compute is increasingly a financial-markets and land-use story rather than only a technology one. Examine the implications of concentrated private AI capex for financial stability and infrastructure governance, and evaluate how India should position itself in this race.

stories.headline: IndusInd ends ex-CEO's employment; Modi turns heat on India Inc over jobs
stories.summary: IndusInd Bank has terminated the employment of its former MD & CEO Sumant Kathpalia and is moving to recover a portion of the pay already paid to him — an unusually public accountability step by a private lender whose derivatives-accounting lapses had already drawn regulatory scrutiny. The move came in the same week that Prime Minister Narendra Modi, addressing an industry gathering, said corporate leaders' "appetite is so insatiable, no matter how much you are given, it is never enough", effectively conceding that the sharp corporate tax cuts of recent years had not translated into higher salaries or new jobs. Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi seized on the remark as the government's "own confession" on the employment record. On the business side, Bank of Maharashtra's MD & CEO said the state-run lender is exploring an asset-management company (AMC) venture and an overseas bond issue, pointing to PSU banks' push into fee-based and offshore funding. Separately, a Deccan Herald analysis examined why several Indian tycoons wanted at home remain resident and welcome abroad, underlining weak enforcement and extradition outcomes.
stories.whyItMatters: The three strands — boardroom accountability in banking, the fiscal cost of corporate tax concessions, and the failure of growth to convert into wages — sit at the heart of the GS-III debate on jobless growth and the quality of public spending. They also give a ready interview and essay link between corporate governance and inclusive growth.

perspectives.take: Frames it as a governance-and-recovery story: a private bank formally severing ties with its former chief and clawing back pay, with markets watching the regulatory signal.
Business-daily lens on expansion — Bank of Maharashtra's AMC foray and overseas bond plan read as PSU banks chasing fee income and cheaper offshore capital rather than as governance news.
Places PM Modi's tough remarks to India Inc front and centre, framing the story around corporate responsibility for jobs — a political-economy take rather than a market one.
Investigative/analytical angle on fugitive tycoons: contrasts the domestic accountability of a bank chief with the impunity of promoters who are wanted at home yet hosted abroad.
Opposition-centred political framing — Rahul Gandhi's 'your own confession' turns the PM's words into an indictment of the government's employment record.

static.topic: Jobless growth and the employment question
static.whatIsIt: Poverty is measured through NITI Aayog's Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and consumption surveys; employment and unemployment are measured by the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), which reports the Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR), Worker Population Ratio and Unemployment Rate.
static.background: NITI Aayog's National MPI (2021) uses 12 indicators across health, education and living standards. The PLFS has been run by the NSO since 2017-18, releasing quarterly urban and annual all-India estimates, replacing the earlier quinquennial Employment-Unemployment Surveys. India became the world's most populous country in 2023, so the size of the workforce — and the quality of work available to it — has become a central policy concern.
static.socioEconomic: A large share of the workforce remains self-employed or in informal and low-productivity work, so output growth can rise without matching growth in formal, salaried jobs — the 'jobless growth' critique that the Prime Minister's remarks bring into the open.
static.whyInNews: PM Modi said corporate tax concessions had not led to higher salaries or job creation; Rahul Gandhi called the statement the government's 'own confession'.
static.wayForward: Shift the policy focus from headline growth to employment elasticity: labour-intensive manufacturing, construction and care services, apprenticeship-linked skilling, and credible, high-frequency jobs data that lets policy be judged on wages, not just GDP.
prelimsPointers: National MPI covers 3 dimensions — health, education, standard of living — across 12 indicators.
Unemployment Rate = unemployed persons ÷ labour force; LFPR = labour force ÷ population.
PLFS is conducted by the National Statistical Office under MoSPI.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why output growth in India has not translated proportionately into wage growth and formal employment, and evaluate the policy mix needed to make growth employment-intensive.

static.topic: Corporate tax cuts and the quality of fiscal policy
static.whatIsIt: Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxation and expenditure to steer the economy, presented annually through the Union Budget (Article 112) and anchored in prudence by the FRBM Act, 2003.
static.background: The FRBM Act targets fiscal-deficit reduction; the N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP anchor of 60% for general government. The GST Council (Article 279A) is the constitutional body for indirect-tax harmonisation, with GST launched in 2017. In September 2019 the government cut the base corporate tax rate for domestic companies to 22% (about 25.17% with surcharge and cess) and offered 15% for new manufacturing units, forgoing an estimated ₹1.45 lakh crore a year in revenue — a concession justified by expected investment and job creation.
static.socioEconomic: Every rupee forgone in tax is a rupee unavailable for capital expenditure, health or skilling; if the private sector responds with higher profits but not higher investment or payrolls, the fiscal trade-off looks poor in employment terms.
static.whyInNews: The Prime Minister's remark that corporate 'appetite' remains unsatisfied despite concessions revives the debate on whether tax incentives buy investment and jobs or merely boost post-tax profits.
static.wayForward: Link tax incentives to verifiable outcomes (investment, payroll headcount, skilling), protect the capital-expenditure share of the budget, and publish transparent revenue-forgone statements so the cost of each concession is auditable.
prelimsPointers: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts (excluding borrowings).
Finance Commission (Article 280) recommends tax devolution; the 15th FC set the states' share at 41%.
GST Council is constituted under Article 279A; the GST came into force in 2017.
static.mainsAngle: Debate whether corporate tax concessions are an efficient use of fiscal space in a labour-surplus economy, and assess the case for outcome-linked incentives over blanket rate cuts.

static.topic: Accountability of bank leadership: RBI's regulatory toolkit
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Banking & Financial Sector Regulation; Corporate Governance
static.whatIsIt: Private and public sector banks are regulated by the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934 and the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The RBI's 'fit and proper' criteria govern who may serve as MD & CEO, and its compensation guidelines for whole-time directors and material risk takers allow deferral, malus and clawback of variable pay.
static.background: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 empowers the RBI to issue directions to banks (Section 35A), to remove managerial or other persons (Section 36AA) and to supersede a bank's board (Section 36ACA); these powers were extended to cooperative banks in 2020. The RBI's Prompt Corrective Action framework imposes escalating curbs on weak banks. Recent episodes — PMC Bank (2019), Yes Bank's reconstruction (2020), Lakshmi Vilas Bank's amalgamation (2020) — established the template of tight board oversight. In the IndusInd case, the RBI had approved a shorter than board-recommended extension for the MD & CEO, and the bank later disclosed losses arising from lapses in its derivatives accounting.
static.socioEconomic: Governance failures in banks are ultimately borne by depositors and taxpayers, which is why recovery of pay and board accountability are treated as public-interest issues, not merely contractual ones.
static.whyInNews: IndusInd Bank terminated its former MD & CEO's employment and moved to recover part of his remuneration, a rare instance of a private lender invoking pay recovery against a senior executive.
static.wayForward: Strengthen board-level risk committees and audit independence, make deferral and clawback of senior variable pay standard in employment contracts, and ensure timely disclosure of accounting lapses so that accountability follows evidence rather than market pressure.
prelimsPointers: Section 36AA of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 allows the RBI to remove a managerial person; Section 36ACA permits supersession of a bank's board.
The RBI's compensation guidelines for CEOs and material risk takers provide for deferral, malus and clawback of variable pay.
Prompt Corrective Action triggers on capital, asset-quality and leverage thresholds.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether India's bank-regulation toolkit gives the RBI and bank boards sufficient means to enforce individual accountability for governance and accounting failures in private banks.

prelims: IndusInd Bank has ended the employment of former MD & CEO Sumant Kathpalia and is seeking to recover part of his pay.
PM Modi said corporate leaders' 'appetite is so insatiable, no matter how much you are given, it is never enough', in effect conceding that tax cuts had not raised salaries or created jobs.
Bank of Maharashtra is exploring an asset management company (AMC) business and an overseas bond issue.
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 empowers the RBI to remove managerial persons (Section 36AA) and to supersede a bank's board (Section 36ACA).
stories.mainsQuestion: Corporate tax concessions and record profits have not been matched by wage growth or job creation in India. Critically examine the reasons for this disconnect and suggest the elements of a genuinely employment-intensive growth strategy.

stories.headline: Drought, cyclone and conservation pressures test environmental governance
stories.summary: Karnataka High Court has directed the state government to identify forests and forest-like areas, even as conservation and livelihood tensions surfaced in West Bengal's Buxa Tiger Reserve after a tigress was translocated and tourism curbs were imposed. Odisha was surprised by Cyclone Akvan, while drought conditions in Karnataka intensified groundwater depletion and prompted the state to promise Rs 5,000 in aid to farmers by December 1. India also developed its first indigenous H5N1 vaccine for poultry, and a Scroll.in interview highlighted the human toll of air pollution. Together, the developments underline overlapping pressures on environmental governance, disaster preparedness and public health.
stories.whyItMatters: These developments link core UPSC themes: conservation versus community rights, disaster management, monsoon variability, groundwater stress and biosecurity. They are useful for GS-I geography, GS-II governance, and GS-III environment and science questions.

static.topic: Forest identification, tiger translocation and community rights
static.whatIsIt: Conservation governance covers legal protection of forests and wildlife, species reintroduction, and balancing tourism and community rights under the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Forest Conservation Act 1980, Biological Diversity Act 2002 and the Forest Rights Act.
static.background: Project Tiger (1973) and Project Elephant (1992) anchor species conservation; the Ramsar Convention (1971) protects wetlands; the CBD (1992) and Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) set the 30x30 target. India is one of 17 megadiverse countries.

static.socioEconomic: Forest villagers often depend on tourism and forest produce; restrictions can affect livelihoods and raise Forest Rights Act and human-wildlife conflict concerns.
static.whyInNews: Karnataka HC ordered identification of forests and forest-like areas; a tigress translocation in Buxa triggered protests over tourism curbs; black leopard conservation was highlighted.
static.wayForward: Participatory conservation, transparent tourism regulation, timely settlement of community rights, and scientific monitoring of translocated animals.

static.topic: Cyclone Akvan, drought and groundwater stress
static.whatIsIt: The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by differential heating, the ITCZ shift and the Tibetan Plateau's heat pump; it delivers about 75% of annual rainfall during June–September. Cyclones and droughts are extreme expressions of monsoon variability.
static.background: El Niño usually weakens the monsoon; La Niña strengthens it; the Indian Ocean Dipole modulates it. The Western Ghats and Himalayan rivers define drainage; peninsular rivers are rain-fed.
static.geography: Odisha coast on the Bay of Bengal for Cyclone Akvan; Karnataka for drought and groundwater depletion.
static.socioEconomic: Drought affects farm incomes, drinking water and groundwater; Karnataka announced Rs 5,000 aid per farmer. Cyclones cause loss of life, property and infrastructure damage.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Akvan surprised Odisha; drought intensified groundwater depletion; Karnataka said drought aid would reach farmers by December 1.
static.wayForward: Strengthen early warning, cyclone shelters, groundwater recharge, crop insurance and climate-resilient agriculture.
prelimsPointers: Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow-fed); peninsular rivers are seasonal.
Western Ghats lie west of the Deccan; highest peak Anamudi (Kerala).
India receives about 75% of annual rainfall during June–September.
static.mainsAngle: Monsoon variability and climate change; disaster preparedness for floods and cyclones.

static.topic: Indigenous H5N1 vaccine and avian influenza biosecurity
static.whatIsIt: H5N1 is a subtype of avian influenza virus that can cause disease in poultry and occasionally spill over to humans. An indigenous poultry vaccine is a biosecurity tool to reduce outbreaks and economic losses.
static.background: Avian influenza outbreaks have led to culling and trade restrictions in several countries. The One Health approach links human, animal and environmental health.
static.socioEconomic: Poultry is a major livelihood source; outbreaks affect farmers, prices and exports. Vaccination can reduce losses but requires cold chain and surveillance.
static.whyInNews: India developed its first indigenous H5N1 vaccine to protect poultry from bird flu.
static.wayForward: Combine vaccination with surveillance, farm biosecurity, compensation for culling and One Health coordination.
prelimsPointers: H5N1 is a subtype of influenza A virus.
Avian influenza is a zoonotic disease.
One Health recognises links between human, animal and environmental health.

stories.headline: US court sentences Nikhil Gupta to 19-plus years in Pannun murder plot case
stories.summary: A US federal court in Manhattan sentenced Indian national Nikhil Gupta to 235 months — a little over 19 years — in prison for his role in a conspiracy to assassinate Khalistani separatist leader Pannun on American soil. US District Judge Victor Marrero pronounced the sentence at a hearing on Friday, according to reports. The case stems from a US indictment alleging a murder-for-hire plot against a US-based Sikh separatist, and it has been a persistent irritant in India–US relations. New Delhi has denied any policy of targeting dissidents abroad and constituted a high-level committee to examine the inputs shared by Washington. The sentencing keeps the themes of transnational repression, diaspora security and legal cooperation between the two democracies in sharp focus.
stories.whyItMatters: The case tests the India–US framework for extradition, mutual legal assistance and counter-terrorism cooperation, while raising larger questions on transnational repression, sovereignty and diaspora safety — a recurring UPSC theme under GS-II International Relations and GS-III Internal Security.

static.topic: Khalistan Movement and Diaspora Extremism

static.whatIsIt: The Khalistan demand for a separate Sikh state, which peaked as an armed insurgency in Punjab in the 1980s–90s and has since resurfaced mainly as diaspora-based political campaigning and referendum-style mobilisation abroad.
static.background: The demand was articulated in the Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973). Militancy intensified after Operation Blue Star (1984) and the events of that period, and Punjab saw a prolonged insurgency through the late 1980s and early 1990s before normalisation. In recent years, overseas groups such as Sikhs for Justice have run 'Referendum 2020'-style campaigns; SFJ was banned in India under the UAPA in 2019.

static.socioEconomic: Diaspora funding, remittances, social-media mobilisation and immigration-linked politics in host countries shape the movement's visibility, even as Punjab's own economy and security situation has been stable for decades.
static.whyInNews: The US sentencing in the alleged plot against a Khalistani separatist has revived attention on the movement and its overseas networks.
static.wayForward: Combine firm legal action against designated extremist outfits with political outreach to diaspora communities, and pursue coordinated counter-extremism engagement with Canada, the US, the UK and Australia.

static.mainsAngle: Discuss why Punjab remains stable while diaspora-based Khalistan mobilisation persists, and evaluate India's mix of legal, diplomatic and outreach responses.

static.topic: Extraterritorial Jurisdiction, Sovereignty and International Law

static.whatIsIt: The legal principles by which a state claims jurisdiction over conduct with a territorial, national or protective link to it — the basis on which the US prosecuted a conspiracy targeting a person on its soil.
static.background: The Permanent Court of International Justice's Lotus case (1927) recognised wide latitude for states in asserting jurisdiction where effects are felt within their territory. The UN Charter's Article 2(4) protects territorial sovereignty and political independence, while the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (1961) governs the immunity of diplomatic personnel — a framework frequently invoked in disputes over alleged foreign interference.

static.wayForward: Strengthen treaty-based channels — extradition, MLAT, mutual legal assistance in criminal matters — so that jurisdictional disputes are resolved through law rather than diplomatic friction.
prelimsPointers: The Lotus case (France v Turkey) was decided by the Permanent Court of International Justice in 1927 and is a leading authority on state jurisdiction.
Article 2(4) of the UN Charter prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.
The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (1961) codifies diplomatic privileges and immunities.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse how competing claims of extraterritorial jurisdiction strain bilateral relations, and assess whether existing extradition and mutual legal assistance treaties are adequate for transnational security cases.

stories.headline: Supreme Court rulings touch RERA liability, jobs and judicial conduct
stories.summary: On 20 November 2026 the Supreme Court delivered a clutch of orders spanning judicial administration, statutory liability and service law. It directed a probe into why its own Registry refused to list an Enforcement Directorate plea against bail for over three years, and issued notice to an advocate over remarks against the Chief Justice. In separate matters, the Court held that a builder's RERA violations cannot fasten criminal liability on lenders, and struck down Uttar Pradesh provisions that excluded work-charged employees' pre-regularisation service from being counted. It also sought the Centre's response on a plea flagging the health risks of consanguineous marriages and the need for public awareness. Elsewhere, a visually impaired Jammu & Kashmir High Court advocate continued a strike over appointment as a law officer, and former Justice Yashwant Verma told Parliament that impeachment proceedings against him had become infructuous after his resignation.
stories.whyItMatters: The day's orders together test three exam-critical themes: judicial administration and delay, the scope of criminal liability under RERA, and the constitutional machinery for judicial accountability and removal. static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power of courts to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction, and Article 142 gives the SC power to do complete justice.
static.socioEconomic: Pendency and vacancy in the higher judiciary affect access to justice, contract enforcement and the cost of litigation for ordinary citizens.
static.whyInNews: The Court ordered a probe into its Registry's refusal to list an ED plea against bail for over three years, and issued notice to an advocate over remarks against the Chief Justice — both raising questions of court administration and conduct.
static.wayForward: Streamline listing and case-flow management through e-filing and strict timelines, fill judicial vacancies, and balance judicial independence with transparent internal accountability.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction: disputes between the Centre and states under Article 131.
Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is under Article 143.
static.mainsAngle: Examine judicial backlog, vacancies and pendency; the balance between judicial independence and accountability.

static.topic: Judicial Accountability and Removal of Judges
static.whatIsIt: A judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court may be removed only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity, through a motion passed by both Houses of Parliament by a special majority and presented to the President.
static.background: The procedure flows from Articles 124(4) and 217(1)(b) read with the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, which provides for a three-member inquiry committee. The special majority required is a majority of the total membership of each House plus two-thirds of members present and voting. No judge has so far been removed in India; the 1993 motion against Justice V. Ramaswami failed in the Lok Sabha.
static.whyInNews: Former Justice Yashwant Verma told Parliament that impeachment proceedings against him had become infructuous after his resignation, reviving debate on whether resignation should end the accountability process.
static.wayForward: Consider clarifying through law or convention the effect of resignation on pending removal motions, and strengthen in-house procedures of the Supreme Court and High Courts for complaints short of removal.
prelimsPointers: Removal requires a special majority in each House separately, not a joint sitting.
The inquiry committee under the 1968 Act has a Supreme Court judge, a High Court Chief Justice and a distinguished jurist.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether the existing removal mechanism adequately ensures judicial accountability without compromising judicial independence.

static.topic: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA)

static.whatIsIt: RERA is a central statute that regulates the real estate sector, requiring project and agent registration with state Real Estate Regulatory Authorities, mandatory disclosure, and remedies before the Real Estate Appellate Tribunal.
static.background: Enacted in 2016 and brought into force on 1 May 2016, RERA followed long-standing complaints of delayed possession and diversion of funds. It mandates that a defined share of amounts realised from allottees be kept in a separate escrow account, defines carpet area, and provides for penalties and imprisonment for specified contraventions. Section 88 gives it overriding effect over inconsistent state laws.
static.socioEconomic: The Act seeks to protect homebuyers, bring transparency to a large employer sector, and improve access to institutional finance for compliant developers.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court held that a builder's RERA violations cannot make lenders criminally liable, clarifying the limits of vicarious criminal responsibility in real estate projects.
static.wayForward: Strengthen state RERA authorities with adequate staffing and appellate capacity, ensure uniform enforcement, and clearly delineate the liability of promoters, lenders and agents.
prelimsPointers: RERA came into force on 1 May 2016; states and union territories must establish a regulator and an appellate tribunal.
A specified portion of amounts realised from allottees must be deposited in a separate account to cover construction cost.
static.mainsAngle: Assess RERA's implementation a decade on: has it curbed project delays and protected homebuyers, and where does enforcement still fall short?

Writ jurisdiction lies with the Supreme Court under Article 32 and with High Courts under Article 226.

static.topic: India's crude oil production and import dependence
static.whatIsIt: Domestic upstream crude production, dominated by state-owned ONGC and Oil India with private and joint-venture operators, set against a consumption basket that is met overwhelmingly through imports.
static.background: India's upstream sector was opened to private participation through the New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP) from the late 1990s, and later through the Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy (HELP, 2016) with the Open Acreage Licensing Policy (OALP) and revenue-sharing contracts. The Directorate General of Hydrocarbons oversees upstream regulation. Domestic output has broadly stagnated over the past decade even as refining capacity and fuel demand expanded.
static.geography: Key producing areas include Mumbai Offshore, the Krishna-Godavari and Cambay basins, the Assam-Arakan belt (Digboi, Naharkatiya) and the Barmer basin in Rajasthan; major refining hubs include Jamnagar, Koyali, Mathura and Paradip.
static.socioEconomic: The crude import bill shapes the current account deficit, the rupee, the fiscal subsidy burden and retail inflation through pump prices; it also drives energy diplomacy with OPEC, Russia and the United States.
static.whyInNews: A report projects that India's crude oil production could fall by about 20% over the next decade while demand continues to increase, widening import dependence.
static.wayForward: Accelerate exploration in underexplored sedimentary basins, sustain OALP rounds, incentivise enhanced oil recovery, scale ethanol blending and biofuels, expand strategic petroleum reserves, and push electrification and public transport to bend the demand curve.
prelimsPointers: India imports more than 80% of its crude oil requirement; domestic output comes mainly from ONGC and Oil India.
India's strategic petroleum reserves are located at Visakhapatnam, Mangalore and Padur, managed by ISPRL.

static.topic: Electric vehicle adoption and charging infrastructure
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Infrastructure: Energy; Environment — Climate Change Mitigation
static.whatIsIt: The policy and market ecosystem — demand incentives, manufacturing incentives, charging infrastructure and grid readiness — that supports a shift from internal combustion engine vehicles to electric vehicles.
static.background: The FAME India scheme was launched in 2015, with FAME-II from 2019 focusing on public and shared transport and on charging infrastructure. Production Linked Incentive schemes cover automobiles and Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) battery manufacturing, and the PM E-DRIVE scheme was introduced in 2024 to support electric two- and three-wheelers, buses and charging stations. The Ministry of Power issued charging infrastructure guidelines in 2019, revised in 2022, and several states have their own EV policies.

stories.headline: Supreme Court allows one-time Karthigai lamp lighting at Thiruparankundram

By staying the High Court's findings, the apex court has kept the contested factual and legal conclusions in abeyance rather than endorsing or reversing them. The permission is expressly limited to a single occasion, so the position for future years will depend on further judicial orders. The arrangement is therefore an interim accommodation, not a final determination of the rights of the parties.

static.topic: RBI, Forex Reserves and Monetary Policy
static.whatIsIt: The RBI is India's central bank, established in 1935 and nationalised in 1949 under the RBI Act, 1934. It conducts monetary policy through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (2016) with a 4% CPI inflation target (±2%), regulates banks, manages the country's foreign exchange reserves and acts as banker to the government.
static.background: The inflation-targeting MPC framework emerged from the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act. Policy tools include repo/reverse repo, Marginal Standing Facility, Cash Reserve Ratio, Statutory Liquidity Ratio and Open Market Operations. Forex reserves are held as foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position with the IMF, and their rupee value moves with exchange-rate and asset-price revaluation.
static.socioEconomic: Adequate reserves provide import cover, cushion the rupee against external shocks and signal sovereign creditworthiness; revaluation-driven declines do not by themselves indicate capital outflows or stress.
static.whyInNews: Reserves fell $14.21 billion to $705.34 billion on revaluation, while the RBI simultaneously announced conversion/switch of state government securities aggregating ₹10,800 crore face value through auction.
static.wayForward: Maintain comfortable import cover, diversify reserve composition, ensure transparent and well-communicated debt switch auctions, and sustain fiscal-monetary coordination to anchor inflation expectations.
prelimsPointers: Repo is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against securities; reverse repo is the absorbing rate.
The MPC has six members — three from the RBI (Governor as chair) and three external — with the Governor holding a casting vote.
Inflation target is 4% CPI with a 2–6% band, reviewed every five years.
Forex reserves comprise foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position with the IMF.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the RBI balances reserve adequacy, exchange-rate stability and price stability, and assess the limits of monetary tools when reserve movements are driven by valuation rather than flows.

static.topic: State Government Securities and Centre-State Fiscal Relations
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union with powers divided by the Union, State and Concurrent Lists in the Seventh Schedule, residuary powers resting with the Union under Article 248. States raise market borrowings through state government securities (State Development Loans), with the RBI conducting auctions and debt switch/conversion operations on their behalf.
static.background: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) examined Centre-State balance. The Governor (Article 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a recurring flashpoint over assent to Bills (Article 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Article 201). Market borrowing by states is governed by Article 293 and subject to fiscal responsibility legislation.
static.socioEconomic: State borrowing costs reflect market perceptions of fiscal health; conversion/switch operations let states re-profile debt, manage redemption bunching and potentially lower interest costs, while deepening the sub-national bond market.
static.whyInNews: The RBI announced that state governments will convert/switch securities aggregating ₹10,800 crore in face value through auction, with security-wise details released.
static.wayForward: Deepen and widen the state bond market, improve disclosure on state contingent liabilities, and strengthen cooperative fiscal frameworks so that debt operations reinforce rather than substitute for fiscal discipline.
prelimsPointers: On the Concurrent List, union law prevails in case of repugnancy unless the state law is reserved for the President's assent (Article 254).
The Inter-State Council (Article 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
State government securities (SDLs) are issued through RBI-conducted auctions; conversion/switch operations replace existing securities with new ones.
static.mainsAngle: Assess how market-based state borrowing and RBI debt-management operations shape fiscal federalism, and whether they strengthen or constrain state autonomy.

static.background: The FPI regime was streamlined under the SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations, 2014, consolidating earlier FII and sub-account categories. In 2023, SEBI introduced an enhanced/additional disclosure framework for certain high-risk FPIs with concentrated holdings, aimed at identifying beneficial owners behind opaque structures.
static.socioEconomic: FPI flows influence equity valuations, the rupee and current-account financing; easing entry improves the ease of doing business and cost of capital, but concentrated or opaque flows raise hot-money and beneficial-ownership concerns.
static.whyInNews: SEBI has proposed removing the additional disclosure framework for FPIs, a potential relaxation of compliance requirements for foreign investors.
static.wayForward: Balance ease of market access with robust KYC and beneficial-ownership verification, using targeted risk-based tools rather than blanket disclosure layers, and monitor flow volatility through macroprudential buffers.

FPIs invest in Indian securities through registered intermediary channels; the framework was consolidated under the 2014 FPI Regulations.
SEBI's 2023 additional disclosure norms targeted FPIs with concentrated or high-risk holdings.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the trade-off between attracting foreign portfolio capital and safeguarding market integrity, and evaluate whether disclosure-based tools or macroprudential measures are better suited to managing FPI risk.

static.background: Parliament (Art. 79) consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, and a Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Art. 111). Money Bills (Art. 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha. Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinise Bills and departmental working, including expenditure, while the CAG audits government accounts and reports to Parliament through the Public Accounts Committee.
static.socioEconomic: Steep-discount bidding can compromise quality and cause project delays, raising the ultimate cost to the exchequer.
static.whyInNews: Officials plan to scrutinise rock-bottom bids across large infrastructure projects and the procurement of goods and services.
static.wayForward: Adopt life-cycle costing, pre-qualification norms and quality-cum-cost-based selection, backed by stronger ex-post audit.
prelimsPointers: Money Bills originate only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha can delay but not amend them on money provisions.
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how procurement design and parliamentary audit together determine value for money in public spending.
